module_title: Baking Cassava Bread Without an Oven

lessons.title: Building a simple charcoal or firewood oven
lessons.body: To build a simple charcoal or firewood oven, you need a metal drum (like a 200-litre oil drum), sand, clay, bricks, and a metal grate. First, cut a door about 30 cm by 30 cm near the bottom of the drum. This is where you will load fuel and place bread. Inside, create a shelf using a metal grate or stones to hold the bread above the fire. Line the bottom with a layer of sand or clay to protect the metal from burning through. For the outer structure, stack bricks or stones around the drum, leaving the door open. Fill gaps with clay or mud to insulate. The chimney can be a metal pipe attached to a hole at the top of the drum, directing smoke away. To use it, burn charcoal or firewood in the bottom until the oven is hot (about 200-220Â°C). You can test heat by sprinkling a little flour on the grate; it should brown in 30 seconds. Then place your cassava bread dough on the grate, close the door (use a metal sheet), and bake. A 500g loaf takes about 40-50 minutes. This oven costs little and uses local materials. Keep it dry and repair cracks with clay after each use. Always have a fire extinguisher or sand bucket nearby for safety.

lessons.title: Using a pot-on-pot method for baking bread
lessons.body: The pot-on-pot method is a simple way to bake cassava bread using two pots: a large pot with a lid (the oven) and a smaller pot or metal stand to hold the bread above the heat. You need a large cooking pot (at least 10 litres), a smaller pot or a metal trivet, and a lid that fits the large pot. First, place a layer of sand or small stones (about 2 cm deep) at the bottom of the large pot. This distributes heat evenly. Put the smaller pot or trivet on top of the sand. Preheat the large pot over a fire or charcoal stove for 10-15 minutes with the lid on. Meanwhile, shape your cassava dough into a round loaf about 5 cm thick. Once the pot is hot, carefully place the dough on the small pot or trivet. Cover with the lid. Place the whole setup over medium heat (charcoal or firewood). Bake for 30-40 minutes. To check, lift the lid after 30 minutes; the bread should be golden brown and sound hollow when tapped. If not, bake 10 more minutes. This method works because the sand insulates and the small pot raises the bread off direct heat, preventing burning. Itâs perfect for small-scale baking. Always use a thick cloth to handle hot pots. Clean the sand after each use and store the pots dry.

lessons.title: Baking cassava bread in a sandbox oven
lessons.body: A sandbox oven is a simple, effective way to bake cassava bread using a box, sand, and a heat source. You need a wooden or metal box (about 60 cm x 60 cm x 60 cm), clean sand, a metal tray or stone slab, and charcoal or firewood. First, fill the box with 10 cm of sand. Place a metal tray or flat stones on top of the sand to hold the bread. Build a fire using charcoal in a metal container (like an old pot) and place it at one end of the box, or use a firewood fire outside and shovel hot coals into the box. Cover the box with a lid or metal sheet to trap heat. Let it heat for 20-30 minutes until the sand is hot (you can feel warmth through the lid). Then place your cassava dough on the tray. Cover again. The sand will hold heat steadily. Bake for 35-45 minutes. Check after 30 minutes: the bread should be firm and browned. If you need more heat, add hot coals through a small opening. This oven is cheap and portable. Itâs ideal for areas with limited resources. After baking, let the fire die out and remove ashes. Store sand dry. Never use wet sand, as it creates steam and uneven baking.

lessons.title: Controlling heat and timing for even baking
lessons.body: Controlling heat and timing is critical for even baking of cassava bread. Cassava dough is dense and needs steady, moderate heat (180-200Â°C) for 40-50 minutes. Too high heat burns the crust before the inside cooks; too low heat makes the bread dry and hard. To control heat in a charcoal or firewood oven, adjust the amount of fuel and the airflow. Start with a good bed of hot coals, then add small pieces of wood or charcoal as needed. Use a metal door or damper to control air. If the oven gets too hot, open the door slightly for 2-3 minutes. If too cool, add more fuel. For pot-on-pot, keep the fire medium; you can move the pot to a cooler part of the fire. For sandbox, add or remove hot coals. Timing: always preheat your oven for at least 20 minutes. Place the bread in the centre. For a 500g loaf, bake 45 minutes. For a 1kg loaf, 60-70 minutes. Rotate the bread halfway through if your oven has hot spots. Use a simple test: after 30 minutes, insert a thin stick into the centre; if it comes out clean, itâs done. If not, bake 10 more minutes. Keep a clock or timer. Write down what you did each time so you can repeat good results. With practice, you will learn your ovenâs behaviour.

lessons.title: Testing bread doneness without a thermometer
lessons.body: You donât need a thermometer to test if cassava bread is done. Use your senses and simple tools. First, the colour: the crust should be golden brown, not pale or dark. Second, the sound: tap the bottom of the loaf with your knuckles. If it sounds hollow, itâs likely done. Third, the stick test: insert a thin wooden stick or skewer into the centre. If it comes out clean or with dry crumbs, itâs done. If it has wet dough, bake longer. Fourth, the touch: press the top gently; it should spring back. If it leaves an indentation, it needs more time. Fifth, the smell: a done loaf smells nutty and toasted, not raw. For cassava bread, because itâs dense, also check the sides: they should pull away slightly from the pan or tray. If youâre unsure, take the bread out, let it cool for 5 minutes, then cut a small slice from the centre. If itâs still doughy, return it to the oven for 10 minutes. Remember, overbaking makes it hard; underbaking makes it gummy. Practise with small loaves first. Keep a record of times and results. Soon youâll judge doneness by look and feel alone.

lessons.title: Cooling and slicing cassava bread loaves
lessons.body: Cooling and slicing cassava bread properly is important for texture and taste. After baking, remove the loaf from the oven and place it on a wire rack or clean cloth. Do not slice immediatelyâhot bread is fragile and steamy inside. Let it cool for at least 30 minutes for a small loaf, 1 hour for a large one. This allows the inside to set and the moisture to redistribute. If you cut too early, the bread will crumble and seem doughy. While cooling, cover loosely with a clean cloth to keep the crust soft, but donât wrap tightly or condensation will make it soggy. For slicing, use a sharp, serrated knife. A bread knife works best. Cut with a gentle sawing motion, not pressing down hard. For even slices, start at one end and cut 1-2 cm thick slices. If the bread is very dense, you can warm the knife slightly. Cassava bread is best eaten fresh, but you can store it in a paper bag for 2 days or freeze for up to 1 month. To reheat, wrap in foil and warm in a pot-on-pot oven for 10 minutes. Always cool completely before storing to prevent mould. With practice, youâll get clean slices every time.

quiz.q: What is the first step in building a simple charcoal or firewood oven from a metal drum?
options: A) Cut a door near the bottom
B) Fill the drum with water
D) Add a chimney at the bottom
quiz.explanation: The door is needed to load fuel and place bread.

quiz.q: In a drum oven, what is the purpose of lining the bottom with sand or clay?
options: B) To protect the metal from burning through
C) To make the oven heavier
quiz.explanation: Sand or clay acts as insulation and prevents the metal from burning.

quiz.q: How can you test if a drum oven is hot enough before baking?
options: A) Touch the metal with your hand
B) Sprinkle a little flour on the grate; it should brown in 30 seconds
C) Pour water on the fire
D) Listen for a whistling sound
quiz.explanation: Flour browning quickly indicates the oven is around 200-220Â°C.

quiz.q: What is the approximate baking time for a 500g cassava loaf in a drum oven?
quiz.explanation: A 500g loaf typically takes 40-50 minutes at moderate heat.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a fire extinguisher or sand bucket near your oven?
options: B) For safety in case of fire
C) To add sand to the bread
quiz.explanation: Safety is crucial when working with fire.

quiz.q: In the pot-on-pot method, what is placed at the bottom of the large pot?
options: B) A layer of sand or small stones
quiz.explanation: Sand or stones distribute heat evenly.

quiz.q: What is the role of the smaller pot or trivet in the pot-on-pot method?
options: A) To hold the bread above direct heat
quiz.explanation: It raises the bread so it doesn't burn on the bottom.

quiz.q: How long should you preheat the large pot in the pot-on-pot method?
quiz.explanation: Preheating for 10-15 minutes ensures the pot is hot enough.

quiz.q: What is a sign that cassava bread is done in the pot-on-pot method?
options: B) It sounds hollow when tapped
quiz.explanation: A hollow sound indicates the bread is baked through.

quiz.q: What type of heat is recommended for the pot-on-pot method?
quiz.explanation: Medium heat prevents burning and allows even baking.

quiz.q: What material is used to fill a sandbox oven?
quiz.explanation: Sand holds and distributes heat evenly.

quiz.q: How long should you heat a sandbox oven before baking?
quiz.explanation: Heating for 20-30 minutes ensures the sand is hot.

quiz.q: What is placed on top of the sand in a sandbox oven?
options: A) A metal tray or flat stones
quiz.explanation: A tray or stones provide a surface for the bread.

quiz.q: Why should you never use wet sand in a sandbox oven?
options: A) It creates steam and uneven baking
C) It makes the bread sweet
D) It cools the oven too much
quiz.explanation: Wet sand produces steam that can ruin the bread's texture.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of a sandbox oven?
options: B) It is portable and cheap
quiz.explanation: Sandbox ovens are low-cost and can be moved.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature range for baking cassava bread?
quiz.explanation: Cassava bread bakes best at moderate heat around 180-200Â°C.

quiz.q: How can you lower the heat in a charcoal oven if it gets too hot?
options: B) Open the door slightly for 2-3 minutes
C) Pour water on the fire
quiz.explanation: Opening the door releases heat and lowers temperature.

quiz.q: What is a simple test for doneness after 30 minutes of baking?
options: A) Insert a thin stick into the centre; if it comes out clean, it's done
B) Touch the top with your hand
quiz.explanation: The stick test is a reliable way to check if the inside is cooked.

quiz.q: Why is it important to record baking times and results?
options: D) To make the bread sweeter
quiz.explanation: Keeping records helps you learn your oven and improve.

quiz.q: How often should you rotate bread in an oven with hot spots?
quiz.explanation: Rotating halfway ensures even baking.

quiz.q: What is the first sign that cassava bread is done?
options: B) The crust is golden brown
C) It smells like raw dough
quiz.explanation: Golden brown colour indicates proper baking.

quiz.q: What does a hollow sound when tapping the bottom of the loaf indicate?
options: D) The bread is too sweet
quiz.explanation: A hollow sound means the bread is baked through.

quiz.q: If a skewer inserted into the centre comes out with wet dough, what should you do?
options: D) Turn up the heat to maximum
quiz.explanation: Wet dough means it needs more baking time.

quiz.q: How can you tell if bread is underbaked by touch?
options: A) It springs back when pressed
B) It leaves an indentation when pressed
quiz.explanation: Underbaked bread doesn't spring back and leaves a dent.

quiz.q: What should you do if you are unsure if the bread is done?
options: A) Take it out and cut a small slice from the centre
quiz.explanation: Cutting a small slice lets you check the inside without ruining the loaf.

quiz.q: Why is it important to let cassava bread cool before slicing?
options: A) To prevent crumbling and gummy texture
D) To avoid burning your hands
quiz.explanation: Cooling allows the inside to set and moisture to redistribute.

quiz.q: How long should a small loaf cool before slicing?
quiz.explanation: 30 minutes is enough for a small loaf to set.

quiz.q: What type of knife is best for slicing cassava bread?
options: B) A sharp serrated bread knife
quiz.explanation: A serrated knife cuts through dense bread cleanly.

quiz.q: How should you store cassava bread to keep it fresh?
options: A) In a paper bag for 2 days
D) In a plastic bag while hot
quiz.explanation: A paper bag allows some airflow and keeps crust from getting soggy.

quiz.q: What is the best way to reheat cassava bread?
options: A) Wrap in foil and warm in a pot-on-pot oven for 10 minutes
B) Microwave on high for 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: Reheating in a covered pot warms it without drying.
